summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 13.7% of firms in Other services, NAICS 81, which includes grantmaking and civic organizations, reported using AI in the last two weeks in the latest BTOS period, up from 12.6% in the prior period. The survey first asked this question in September 2023, and the figure measures the share of firms answering yes, not the intensity or depth of use.

Candid reports that nearly a quarter of corporate funders support using AI to decide grant approvals and denials, while most see AI for administrative tasks as a way to free up time. CEP's sector research covers how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, though the excerpt provided does not include measured results from that work.

The World of AI catalog lists four individually verified organizations in its nonprofits and open source foundations category, two nonprofits and two open source foundations, and notes that none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a neutral evaluation platform, Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software tools that intersect with AI-generated imagery and 3D content. The page states there are no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data center specifications, and no open model foundations releasing weights for public use, and it records no funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

NTEN frames nonprofit technology as marked by inequities within organizations and the sector, and calls on users, builders, and funders to ensure equitable use of technology. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, transforms public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning environments, and provides standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities. These sources point to access and training gaps as the main risk, while no source in this set reports return on investment evidence or a regulatory posture.

A reader deciding whether to deploy AI in a nonprofit should treat the Census figure as modest and slowly rising, expect administrative use to be the most accepted near term application, and plan for equity and governance capacity as the binding constraints. The catalog suggests nonprofit AI infrastructure is small and not a source of compute or open models, so deployment will likely depend on commercial tools and funder support.

https://cep.org/.brief: The Center for Effective Philanthropy page announces a limited-time discount on 2027 assessments or advisory projects, with savings up to $1000 for signing up before Sept. 30. It promotes a podcast episode where donors Jeff Atwood and Dr. Betsy Burton discuss their commitment to give away $50 million in five years. CEP describes its work offering assessments, data-driven research, customized advisory services, events, and blog commentary to influence foundations and major donors. The page also highlights new data on how nonprofits are faring and how foundations are responding, and features blog posts on topics such as inflation’s impact on grantmaking and deciding when a foundation’s mission requires more spending.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid offers a large database of grants and nonprofit information to help users locate funding opportunities, research organizations, and connect with funders. According to Candid, about 25 % of corporate funders use AI to decide grant approvals and denials. For most funders, Candid reports that “using AI for administrative tasks will free up time.” The site emphasizes its comprehensive data as a resource for those seeking funding or researching nonprofits.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogs four individually verified nonprofit and open-source organizations, each with a sourced classification note. It states that LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform, while Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education, and the Krita and Blender foundations steward creative software tools that intersect with AI-generated imagery and 3D content. The page notes that none of these are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense, and the list excludes training compute providers, standards bodies, and open-model foundations that release weights. It also says the notes confirm only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.
